I’m an aspiring architect and designer interested in science, technology, and environmental issues. I enjoy creative problem-solving and turning ideas into meaningful projects.

I’m looking for teammates skilled in programming, web development, data analysis, or scientific research. I value creativity, responsibility, teamwork, and a willingness to learn. Let’s combine our skills to build something impactful!
summary:
FireCal is a web application that turns 25 years of NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots into one consistent burning activity calendar for Kazakhstan and neighbouring regions. MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) detect fires at different resolutions and sensitivities, so their counts cannot be compared directly. FireCal groups detections from both sensors into the same H3 grid cells and UTC days, then converts the MODIS-only years to the VIIRS scale using month-specific VIIRS/MODIS ratios measured over the years when both sensors were flying. The result is a single series from November 2000 to December 2025 (2.34 million cell-days) in which the sensor of origin no longer matters.

Users draw an area or enter coordinates, pick a period and immediately see a years × months calendar, the selected period compared with the historical median, anomalous days and months, a year-to-year swipe map, and CSV and PNG exports. A machine-learning outlook (LightGBM and a PyTorch neural network using fire history and NASA POWER fire weather) estimates where hotspots are likely in the next 1–7 days. FireCal helps emergency managers, scientists and land managers recognise critical periods and unusual seasons early.
details:
What it does

FireCal is a satellite atlas of burning activity for Kazakhstan and adjacent territory (46–93°E, 40–56°N). It answers three questions for any area and period: when does this place usually burn, was this season unusual, and where are hotspots likely in the coming days.

How it works

1. Data. We downloaded standard-processing Terra/Aqua MODIS and Suomi NPP VIIRS hotspots from the NASA FIRMS Area API for November 2000 – December 2025 and kept vegetation fires (industrial gas flares removed).

2. Harmonization. Detections from both sensors are grouped into H3 resolution-7 cells (~5 km²) and UTC days, so a 1 km MODIS pixel and a 375 m VIIRS pixel describe the same unit: a burning cell-day. For each calendar month we compute the median VIIRS/MODIS ratio over the overlap years (2012–2025) and use it to place the MODIS-only years (2000–2011) on the VIIRS scale. We also detect VIIRS instrument gaps (for example 27 July – 10 August 2022) so they are not mistaken for quiet periods.

3. Burning activity calendar. A years × months heatmap shows the whole record at a glance: counts on one colour scale shared by all years, or a diverging "vs normal" mode comparing each month with its median in other years. A daily calendar, a monthly season chart and a list of the most active cells add detail.

4. Historical comparison. For any selected period FireCal reports the percentage difference from the historical median of the same dates, the rank among all years, and anomalous days or months (z-score against the same calendar month in other years).

5. Hotspot outlook. For every 0.25° cell (12 032 cells) we predict the probability of at least one VIIRS hotspot on the next day and during the next 7 days. Inputs: recent detections, the harmonized seasonal climatology, land cover, the Canadian Fire Weather Index System computed from NASA POWER (MERRA-2) weather, rainfall and soil moisture. Trained on 2013–2021, model selection on 2022, tested on 2023–2025, with 20% of 4° × 4° blocks excluded from training. The PyTorch CNN reaches an average precision of 0.50 for the 7-day outlook compared with 0.33 for seasonal climatology. The 10% highest-risk cells contain 70% of the following week's hotspots, and the probabilities are well calibrated.

6. Interface. A 3D globe entry page, map drawing or coordinate entry, quick period presets, a step-by-step side panel, a swipe map comparing two years, a forecast layer with a "ratio to normal" view, colour-blind-safe palettes, keyboard navigation, light and dark themes, Russian and English, a shareable link to the current view, and CSV/PNG export.

Benefits and intended impact

Fire managers get a consistent 25-year history instead of two incompatible records. They can see which months are critical in their district, whether the current season is above or below normal, and which cells are likely to burn next week. That supports patrol planning, early warning and public communication. Scientists and land managers can export harmonized series for any area.

Tools and technologies

Python (pandas, NumPy, DuckDB, H3, FastAPI, Uvicorn), PyTorch, LightGBM, scikit-learn and SciPy for the data pipeline, backend and models; JavaScript, HTML5 Canvas, WebGL and Leaflet with Leaflet.draw for the web app; NASA FIRMS, NASA POWER and Blue Marble data; ESA WorldCover for land cover.

Creativity

The challenge's "calendar" is implemented literally as a years × months matrix that becomes an anomaly map with one click. The harmonized MODIS + VIIRS climatology is reused as the strongest predictor of the hotspot outlook, which links the historical analysis to early warning. Each model on the leaderboard adds one source of information (climatology, then recent fires, then observed weather, then forecast-window weather), so users see what actually adds skill.

Factors we considered

Satellite detections are not fires: clouds, overpass times and sensor sensitivity affect them. Most hotspots in the region are agricultural and steppe burns. Land cover is a 2021 snapshot. Monthly ratios cannot recover individual small fires that MODIS missed. The outlook backtest uses reanalysis weather as a perfect forecast, and we report a variant that uses only data available on the issue date. These caveats are shown in the app and the README. The archive currently ends on 31 December 2025.
